stem.en: A lab grows thousands of plants of a rare orchid by tissue culture. Nearly all of them are just like the parent plant, but a few have flowers with odd petal shapes. What is the most likely reason for these few plants?

text.en: During a long time in culture, changes can sometimes happen in a few cells, and plants from them differ.

feedback.en: Yes. Plants from tissue culture are usually like the parent. Sometimes, after a long time in culture, a few plants come out a little different.

text.en: Tissue culture always gives plants that differ from the parent, because no two cells are ever alike.

feedback.en: No. Tissue culture is used because it usually gives plants just like the parent. Here only a few plants differ.

text.en: The plants were grown without soil, so they did not get the minerals they needed to form petals.

feedback.en: No. The nutrient medium gives the plants the minerals they need. A lack of minerals would not change the petals of only a few plants.

text.en: Seeds of another kind of orchid fell into the open jars by chance, and those seeds grew into the odd plants.

feedback.en: No. The jars are kept closed and clean. Plants from stray seeds would be a different orchid, not this orchid with odd petals.

explanation.en: Tissue culture usually gives plants just like the parent, which is why nearly all the orchids are normal. When cells are kept in culture for a long time, changes can sometimes happen in a few of them, and the plants that grow from those cells may differ a little. That is why labs check the plants they grow.

hints.en: Are most of the plants normal or odd? What does that tell you about the method?
What is different about life in a culture jar for a long time?
